title: Whole-cell patch clamp and extracellular electrophysiology in mouse brain slices
author: Chen, Shi, et al.

steps.title: Prepare cutting solution
steps.instruction: Make 1 L cutting solution containing (in mM): 220 glycerol, 2.5 KCl, 1.25 NaH2PO4·H2O, 25 NaHCO3, 0.5 CaCl2·2H2O, 7 MgCl2·6H2O, and 20 D‑glucose; add 0.4 mM ascorbic acid. Adjust pH if needed, filter through a 0.2 µm syringe filter, aliquot, store at –20 °C (pre‑freeze 30 mL) and keep the remaining solution on ice (≈0–4 °C). Continuously bubble with 95 % O2 / 5 % CO2 before use.

steps.title: Prepare artificial CSF (aCSF)
steps.instruction: Make 1 L aCSF containing (in mM): 125 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 25 NaHCO3, 1.25 NaH2PO4·H2O, 2.5 CaCl2·2H2O, 1.3 MgCl2·6H2O, 10 D‑glucose, and 0.4 mM ascorbic acid. Adjust pH to 7.35–7.40, filter, store at 4 °C (up to 1 week). Continuously bubble with 95 % O2 / 5 % CO2. For astrocyte recordings reduce CaCl2 to ~1.5 mM; for spontaneous EPSC recordings increase KCl to 3.0–3.5 mM.

steps.title: Prepare intracellular solutions
steps.instruction: a) KCl‑based solution for action potentials and sIPSCs: dissolve 135 mM KCl, 0.5 mM EGTA, 10 mM HEPES, 2 mM Mg‑ATP, 0.2 mM Na‑GTP, 4 mM Na2‑phosphocreatine; adjust pH to 7.25 with KOH/HCl, verify osmolarity 280–290 mOsm, filter (0.2 µm), aliquot, store at –20 °C. b) CsCl‑based solution for mIPSCs: 130 mM CsCl, 5 mM KCl, 0.5 mM EGTA, 10 mM HEPES, 2 mM Mg‑ATP, 0.2 mM Na‑GTP, 4 mM Na2‑phosphocreatine; pH 7.25, 280–290 mOsm, filter, aliquot, store –20 °C. c) Modified Cs/KCl solution for EPSCs: replace half of the CsCl with KCl to obtain 67.5 mM CsCl + 67.5 mM KCl; add QX‑314 to 4 mM. All solutions are filtered and stored as above.

steps.title: Add extracellular pharmacological blockers
steps.instruction: To the aCSF used for IPSC recordings add DNQX to 10 µM and AP5 to 20 µM. For mIPSC/mEPSC recordings add TTX to 1 µM. For EPSC recordings where GABAA receptors must be blocked add picrotoxin to 100 µM (use with caution as it can induce network hyperexcitability).

steps.title: Set up slicing environment
steps.instruction: a) Pre‑freeze 30 mL cutting solution at –20 °C. b) Fill a large ice box with crushed ice; place a 500 mL beaker on ice and add 300 mL cutting solution (kept at 4 °C) continuously bubbled with 95 % O2 / 5 % CO2. c) Prepare a petri dish with scalpel blade and filter paper on ice for brain trimming. d) Place an empty 25 mL beaker on ice for later brain immersion. e) Gather dissection tools (fine‑tipped brush, surgical scissors, broad‑tip tweezers, long‑handed tissue transfer tool with curved and straight ends). f) Load a syringe with 30 mL cold cutting solution for transcardial perfusion. g) Prepare incubation beaker with ~300 mL 4 °C aCSF, place in a 34 °C water bath, and bubble continuously with 95 % O2 / 5 % CO2.

steps.title: Perfuse and dissect mouse brain
steps.instruction: a) Anesthetize mouse with ketamine/xylazine mixture. b) Secure mouse on perfusion tray. c) Perform transcardial perfusion by injecting ~25 mL ice‑cold cutting solution via the right ventricle. d) Quickly decapitate and immerse head in oxygenated ice‑cold cutting solution for 5 s. e) Extract brain carefully to avoid damage. f) Trim brain in a petri dish filled with cutting solution (coronal or horizontal orientation as required). g) Glue trimmed brain onto the vibratome plate using a small amount of “502 super‑glue” (avoid excess).

steps.title: Slice brain and collect sections
steps.instruction: a) Mount brain plate on Leica VT1000S vibratome. b) Secure bottom plate in clamping slot, wait 2–3 s for glue to set. c) Install vibratome blade with ~10° tilt. d) Fill slicing chamber with pre‑oxygenated cutting solution, ensuring full submersion of brain and blade. e) Surround chamber with crushed ice and add –20 °C iced cutting solution to create an ice‑water mixture for rapid cooling. f) Set vibration frequency, slicing speed, and start/stop positions for continuous 300 µm coronal sections. g) Use a brush or pipette to gently collect slices while bubbling oxygen. h) Transfer slices onto the mesh of the incubation chamber, adjust gas flow to keep slices settled and well‑oxygenated. i) Maintain incubation chamber at 34 °C for 30 min, then at room temperature (23 °C) for the remainder of the experiment.

steps.title: Set recording conditions
steps.instruction: a) Transfer a slice to the recording chamber and perfuse continuously with aCSF (including any required blockers). b) Set the whole‑cell patch‑clamp holding potential to –70 mV. c) Apply the appropriate intracellular solution (KCl‑based, CsCl‑based, or modified Cs/KCl) via the patch pipette. d) Ensure access resistance does not increase >15 % during recording; discard cells that exceed this threshold.

steps.title: Acquire and analyze electrophysiological data
steps.instruction: a) Use a MultiClamp 700B amplifier, Digidata 1550B interface, and pClamp 9.2 software to acquire data. b) Analyze recordings with Clampfit 9 (or Mini Analysis for spontaneous synaptic currents). c) Quantify events using threshold and template‑based searches. d) Present data as mean ± SEM. e) Perform statistical comparisons: Student’s t‑test for two groups; one‑way or two‑way ANOVA with Tukey post‑hoc for multiple groups; Kolmogorov‑Smirnov test for cumulative distributions of sEPSCs. f) Exclude cells with >15 % increase in access resistance from analysis.

description: Electrophysiology provides a powerful approach for investigating the electrical properties of neurons and glial cells by enabling direct measurements of membrane potentials, synaptic currents, and network activity. However, its complexity demands extensive training, precise execution, and specialized expertise, which can make it challenging to obtain reliable and reproducible results. This protocol introduces several conceptual and methodological improvements over existing patch-clamp techniques. First, this protocol offers specific adjustments to intra- and extracellular solutions to optimize different types of recordings. For example, we typically maintain extracellular KCl at 2.5 mM to assess basic membrane properties and spiking. Increasing the concentration to 3.0 mM can modestly enhance neuronal excitability and promote spontaneous synaptic release, particularly of excitatory neurotransmitters. Second, we outline detailed brain slicing procedures—including ice-cold perfusion, use of crushed ice during dissection, rapid processing, and application of glycerol/vitamin C-enriched solutions—to maximize tissue viability, reduce oxidative stress and improve slice quality and recording consistency. Third, the protocol combines whole-cell and extracellular recordings (e.g., LTP and CAP) to facilitate a more intuitive understanding of electrophysiological principles at both the cellular and network levels. Representative data and troubleshooting tips further support hands-on learning and help users successfully carry out their own recordings. In summary, the integration of whole-cell and extracellular recording techniques not only supports a range of experimental paradigms but also enables new users to grasp the fundamentals of whole-cell recordings more clearly through direct comparison with extracellular signals.
